```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>",
  fig.width = 7,
  fig.height = 4.5,
  out.width = "100%",
  dpi = 96
)
has_ggplot2 <- requireNamespace("ggplot2", quietly = TRUE)
has_sf <- has_ggplot2 && requireNamespace("sf", quietly = TRUE)
```

Everything in this article works straight after installing bdhs. You don't
need a DHS account or any downloads, because the package ships every official
estimate the DHS Program publishes for Bangladesh. These are the numbers in
the BDHS final reports and in STATcompiler.

```{r setup}
library(bdhs)
```

## What is bundled

`bdhs_indicators` holds about 310,000 official values. That covers every
indicator, every survey round from 1993-94 to 2022, and every published
breakdown: national, division and background characteristics such as
residence, education and wealth.
`bdhs_indicator_catalog` describes each indicator (definition, denominator,
topic and the rounds it covers).

```{r}
nrow(bdhs_indicators)
dplyr::count(bdhs_indicator_catalog, topic, sort = TRUE)
```

## Finding an indicator

`bdhs_search()` looks through indicator labels and definitions, survey
variables and harmonized variables at once. Restrict it to indicators with
`where = "indicators"`:

```{r}
bdhs_search("stunt", where = "indicators")
```

## Pulling official values

`bdhs_official()` returns tidy rows for one or more indicators. By default it
gives the national headline value for every round:

```{r}
bdhs_official("CN_NUTS_C_HA2")[, c("year_label", "indicator", "value", "ci_low", "ci_high")]
```

Ask for a breakdown to get subgroup values, for example by division in 2022:

```{r}
stunting_div <- bdhs_official("CN_NUTS_C_HA2", survey = 2022, breakdown = "subnational")
stunting_div[, c("characteristic_label", "value", "denom_unweighted")]
```

Besides the eight current divisions, the DHS Program also publishes the
older groupings, such as "Chattogram/Sylhet", "Dhaka before 2015" (Dhaka
plus Mymensingh) and "Rajshahi/Rangpur". These match the division layout of
earlier rounds, so they are the values to use for long-run regional trends.

The `survey` argument accepts years, year ranges, DHS ids and file codes, so
`2017`, `"2017-18"`, `"BD2017DHS"` and `"7R"` all mean the 2017-18 survey.

## Trends

`bdhs_plot_trend()` draws an indicator across all rounds. Give it a
characteristic category to split the trend:

```{r, eval = has_ggplot2}
bdhs_plot_trend("FE_FRTR_W_TFR", by = "Residence")
```

Several indicators can share one chart:

```{r, eval = has_ggplot2, fig.height = 5}
bdhs_plot_trend(c("CN_NUTS_C_HA2", "CN_NUTS_C_WH2", "CN_NUTS_C_WA2"))
```

## Maps

`bdhs_boundaries()` returns the division boundaries used by a given survey,
as an `sf` object. They come from the DHS Program Spatial Data Repository
under the Open Database License. The number of divisions changed over time:
5 in 1993-94, 6 from 1996-97, 7 from 2011 (Rangpur) and 8 from 2017-18
(Mymensingh).

```{r, eval = has_sf}
b <- bdhs_boundaries(2022)
b[, c("region_code", "region_name")]
```

`bdhs_map()` draws an official indicator by division:

```{r, eval = has_sf, fig.height = 6.5, fig.width = 5.5}
bdhs_map("CN_NUTS_C_HA2", survey = 2022)
```

It also maps your own estimates. Any data frame with division codes (`v024`,
`hv024`, `region_code`) or division names works, including the output of
`bdhs_estimate(..., by = "v024")`.

## Notes on comparability

* Division layouts differ between rounds, so division-level trends are only
  comparable after back-mapping to a common layout. `bdhs_regions` gives the
  crosswalk, and `bdhs_harmonize()` creates `division_trend6` and
  `division_trend5` for microdata.
* Official values are rounded the way the DHS Program publishes them. Values
  you compute from microdata with `bdhs_estimate()` keep full precision.
* Please cite the DHS Program API when you use these values
  (`citation("bdhs")`).
